Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-01
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Singh (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Lena Chen (Peregrine VP Eng), Raj Patel (Network Lead), Sara O'Neill (InfoSec), Tom Brooks (Cloud Architect)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros - I'm Maya, AE on Redwood, and Carlos our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Lena (Peregrine): Hi, Lena here, looking forward. We've got Raj, Sara and Tom on the line.
[00:18] Carlos (Redwood SE): Great, high level today is to understand your networking constraints for a private deployment - VPC peering, PrivateLink, transit patterns, IP ranges, that sort of thing. We'll try not to get too deep unless you want.

[00:32] Lena: Yeah, main ask is private-only. We can't have public endpoints for our inference traffic. Compliance reasons, data residency. We're evaluating whether Redwood Hosted with Private Connect or Redwood Private in our VPC is the right fit.
[00:44] Maya: Got it. Quick qual - what cloud are you on and regions?
[00:48] Tom: We're primarily on AWS, us-east-1 and eu-west-1. We also have a on-prem colo that routes over Direct Connect.
[00:56] Raj: We manage our own Transit Gateway and prefer centralized egress. Want to make sure any proposal plays nicely with TGW and our route tables.

[01:10] Carlos: Perfect - so two main patterns we typically recommend: 1) Private endpoints via AWS PrivateLink/Interface endpoints where Redwood exposes an ENI inside your VPC and traffic never traverses the public internet; 2) VPC peering/Transit Gateway where you host Redwood Private in a customer-managed VPC or we can peer to a Redwood-managed VPC; if peered, you must control route tables to ensure egress follows your TGW and NATs. There are tradeoffs on scaling and IP consumption.
[01:36] Sara (InfoSec): Can you clarify the difference in egress? We need to avoid surprises where inference calls go out to public subnets for things like model downloads.
[01:44] Carlos: Yeah, good question. For PrivateLink the data path is private - calls to the inference API stay within AWS fabric and the endpoint ENIs are in your subnets. For peering/TGW, you can host Redwood in your account or we can peer to a Redwood-managed VPC; if peered, you must control route tables to ensure egress follows your TGW and NATs. Model artifacts initial sync may require S3 access - we support S3 VPC endpoints and you can host model artifacts in your S3 bucket with access via VPC endpoint policies.
[02:10] Raj: IP space is a concern - our CIDR is fairly small in eu-west-1. How many ENIs / IPs does PrivateLink consume per AZ?
[02:18] Carlos: It's roughly one ENI per AZ per endpoint per AZ that you enable. For high-availability across 3 AZs, expect 3 ENIs and associated private IPs. If you're tight on IPs we might recommend host-in-customer-account pattern or shared TGW attachment to reduce extra IPs.

[02:36] Lena: What's the path for dedicated capacity? We want predictable throughput for low-latency calls.
[02:42] Maya: Redwood Dedicated or Private can be deployed into your VPC with pinned GPU capacity. Dedicated capacity gives you reserved GPU pools; private deployment in customer VPC gives full network control. For latency we recommend colocating in same region and AZs as your app tiers.
[02:56] Tom: And region constraints - we need eu-west-1 strictly for some workloads. Do you have PV offering in eu-west-1?
[03:02] Carlos: We support private deployments in eu-west-1; availability depends on capacity and model requirements. For some newer GPU types we may have limited availability; we can surface a capacity calendar. For hosted private endpoints we support endpoints in those regions as well.

[03:20] Sara: KMS - we need customer-managed keys, HSM-backed if possible, and rotation policies. How does Redwood integrate?
[03:28] Carlos: We integrate with AWS KMS; for private deployments inside your VPC we can use your KMS keys exclusively. For hosted PrivateLink there's a handshake - we can accept envelope encryption backed by customer CMKs in cross-account setups but the typical approach is customer-hosted VPC + CMK. If HSM-level is required we can discuss HSM integrations and enterprise plan.

[03:50] Raj: Logging and audit trails - we need request-level audit logs and per-call metadata retained for 90 days. How do you expose logs?
[03:58] Maya: In Redwood Console we surface per-route logs, tracing hooks, and you can stream logs to your SIEM via Kinesis / CloudWatch or to a private S3. For Private deployments logs can stay in your account; for hosted we stream logs to your destination over secure channels.

[04:18] Tom: What about network ACLs and security groups? Any required ports?
[04:22] Carlos: TCP/443 for API calls; the ENIs will need security group rules to allow your app subnets to reach them. For model pull we use HTTPS to S3 endpoints; if you have strict firewall rules we can provide the IP ranges used for model synchronization, but we prefer VPC endpoints for S3 to avoid IP exceptions.

[04:40] Lena: If we go with PrivateLink vs peering, what are the operational differences? Which one is easier for us to manage?
[04:46] Carlos: PrivateLink is simpler from a security perspective: it's just an interface endpoint and you control security groups. It's also cross-account friendly. Peering/TGW gives more control and lower per-request latency potentially, but requires route table management and careful CIDR planning. Peering can also make troubleshooting more complex for egress.

[05:06] Raj: Our Transit Gateway enforces NAT egress through a central firewall; will PrivateLink bypass that?
[05:12] Carlos: PrivateLink endpoints are in your subnet so traffic to them stays local; whether it hits your central egress depends on your routing. If your routing sends traffic to TGW for all destinations, you can ensure it goes through firewall. For peering, you control the route to send to TGW as usual.

[05:28] Maya: Quick note on performance - for low-latency small payloads, using a dedicated GPU pool in your VPC gives best predictability. We can run a benchmark with representative queries.
[05:38] Lena: Yes please - we'd like a latency profile at 64/128 tokens and a throughput run.

[05:44] Carlos: We'll need sample prompts and expected qps, and we'll recommend batching settings. For cost, quantization and batch size will be tradeoffs.

[05:58] Sara: Any external callouts to third-party telemetry or health endpoints?
[06:02] Carlos: No outbound telemetry by default. Healthchecks can be exposed to your private subnets; we don't ship customer payloads to third parties.

[06:10] Tom: On the subject of failover across regions - if we have us-east primary and eu-west for DR, can the private endpoint route cross-region?
[06:18] Carlos: Cross-region PrivateLink isn't a thing; you'd provision endpoints per region. For failover you'd need a multi-region deployment or DNS-based failover to the other region's endpoint. We can support multi-region model sync but it requires replication of artifacts to secondary S3 and the usual replication configs.

[06:36] Raj: We also use strict IP allowlists for outgoing traffic from our VPCs. Will Redwood provide stable IPs if we host in our VPC?
[06:44] Maya: If Redwood runs inside your account, you control egress NATs and IPs. If you consume a Redwood-managed VPC via PrivateLink, we can provide the ENI IPs but they can change; best practice is to use VPC endpoints or peering to keep control of egress.

[06:58] Lena: Are there any compliance docs you can share right away?
[07:02] Maya: Yes - I'll send SOC2, ISO attestation, and our network checklist. Carlos will include the network diagram template.

[07:10] Carlos: Also I'll put together an example route table and security group config for PrivateLink and for a hosted-in-customer-account deployment.

[07:18] (brief cross-talk)

[07:24] Raj: For the pilot, what's the simplest setup? We want to minimize ops effort first.
[07:28] Maya: Easiest is PrivateLink - you create interface endpoints in an app subnet we recommend, open port 443 to Redwood security group, and we can spin up a small dedicated pool in that region. No peering or TGW changes needed.

[07:40] Tom: That sounds good for an initial test. If we need to go full private hosting later we can look at bringing the instances into our account.

[07:48] Carlos: One caveat - PrivateLink will consume ENI/IPs and we recommend at least three AZs for HA. If you're IP-constrained, consider the host-in-customer-account route.

[08:00] Lena: Ok - timeline. We're aiming to start a pilot in two weeks. Can you support that?
[08:06] Maya: Yes, we'll target the pilot. Action items: we'll send docs, you'll send CIDRs and TGW info, and we'll schedule the technical deep-dive/benchmark.

[08:16] Sara: Last question - data retention and deletion. If we host models, how do we ensure data isn't kept longer than allowed?
[08:24] Carlos: We support per-customer retention policies; for private deployments you can control retention in your account. For hosted, we enforce tenant-level retention controls and can show audit logs. We'll include specifics in the security pack.

[08:36] Maya: Great - thanks everyone. Anything else?
[08:40] Tom: No, that's it for me.
[08:44] Lena: Thanks, appreciate it.

[08:48] Maya: We'll follow up with the docs and propose times for the deep dive.

End of call.
